intro: Voice decides who stands at the front of the sentence and who really acts. In the passive (れる / られる) the subject undergoes an action that someone else does; in the causative (せる / させる) the subject makes or lets someone else act; in the causative-passive (させられる) the subject is made to act. させてください and させてもらう use the causative to ask for, or receive, permission to act yourself. The last skill of the group, ないで / なくて / ずに, is how a negative verb links to the next clause. Before choosing, ask one question: who actually does the action of the verb?

skills.rule: Passive = the subject undergoes the action and the doer takes に; godan -u becomes -areru, ichidan adds られる, する becomes される, 来る becomes 来られる.
skills.explain:
The passive puts the one who undergoes the action at the front and marks the doer with に. Godan verbs change the final -u to -areru (書く→書かれる, 言う→言われる, 盗む→盗まれる); ichidan verbs add られる (見る→見られる); する→される; 来る→来られる. The result conjugates like an ichidan verb.

Japanese uses the passive mainly when something happens to a person, and very often the effect is unwelcome. Even intransitive verbs make this 'it happened to me' passive: 雨に降られた, 'I got caught in the rain'; 赤ちゃんに泣かれた, 'the baby cried and I suffered for it'. When the thing affected is your belonging or body part, you stay the subject and the thing keeps を: 財布を盗まれた, 足を踏まれた.

Facts about things also take the passive: この寺は八百年前に建てられた. A maker or author takes によって, not に: この本は有名な作家によって書かれた. For ichidan verbs the passive looks the same as the potential (食べられる); a doer marked with に shows it is passive.
patterns: [doer] に [intransitive verb, passive] (it happened to me)

examples.jp: 私[わたし]は先生[せんせい]に{褒[ほ]められました}。
examples.en: I was praised by my teacher.

examples.jp: 弟[おとうと]は犬[いぬ]に{かまれました}。
examples.en: My younger brother was bitten by a dog.

examples.jp: 電車[でんしゃ]で財布[さいふ]を{盗[ぬす]まれました}。
examples.en: I had my wallet stolen on the train.

examples.jp: 帰[かえ]りに雨[あめ]に{降[ふ]られて}、びしょびしょになった。
examples.en: I got caught in the rain on the way home and got soaked.

examples.jp: この寺[てら]は八百年前[はっぴゃくねんまえ]に{建[た]てられました}。
examples.en: This temple was built eight hundred years ago.

examples.jp: 夜中[よなか]に赤[あか]ちゃんに{泣[な]かれて}、全然[ぜんぜん]寝[ね]られなかった。
examples.en: The baby cried in the night, and I couldn't sleep at all.

contrast.note: 書かれた is 'it was written (by someone)'; 書かせた is 'I made or let someone write'. The passive receives; the causative sends.
For godan verbs the shapes differ: 書かれる is passive, 書ける is 'can write'. For ichidan verbs 食べられる is both; a doer with に means passive; an object with が or を and no doer means 'can'.
待たれた is 'someone waited for me' (and it bothered me); 待たされた is 'I was kept waiting'.

mistakes.bad: 先生[せんせい]が私[わたし]に{褒[ほ]められました}。
mistakes.good: 私[わたし]は先生[せんせい]に{褒[ほ]められました}。
mistakes.note: The one who receives the action is the subject; the doer takes に. The bad sentence says the teacher was praised by me.

mistakes.bad: 電車[でんしゃ]で私[わたし]の足[あし]が{踏[ふ]まれました}。
mistakes.good: 電車[でんしゃ]で足[あし]を{踏[ふ]まれました}。
mistakes.note: When your body or belongings are affected, you are the subject and the part keeps を.

mistakes.bad: 帰[かえ]りに雨[あめ]が{降[ふ]られました}。
mistakes.good: 帰[かえ]りに雨[あめ]に{降[ふ]られました}。
mistakes.note: In the 'it happened to me' passive the rain is the doer, so it takes に; the unstated subject is you.

skills.tip: Find the doer: if it is marked with に and the subject just suffers or receives, use the passive.

skills.rule: Causative (せる / させる) = the subject makes or lets someone act; causative-passive (させられる, short godan form -asareru) = the subject is made to act by someone marked with に.
skills.explain:
Godan: -u → -aseru (書く→書かせる, 待つ→待たせる, 言う→言わせる); ichidan: る→させる (食べさせる); する→させる; 来る→来させる. The person made to act takes を with an intransitive verb (弟を買い物に行かせた) and に when the verb already has a を object (子どもに野菜を食べさせた). 'Make' or 'let' comes from context: 好きなだけ遊ばせた is 'let'. Feelings work too: 母を心配させた, 'I worried my mother'.

The causative-passive turns this round: the subject is made to do something, usually unwillingly. Add られる to the causative: 食べさせられる, させられる, 来させられる. Godan verbs normally contract -aserareru to -asareru: 書かされる, 待たされる, 飲まされる. Verbs ending in す cannot contract: 話させられる, never 話さされる. The one who forced you takes に: 先輩にお酒を飲まされた.

examples.jp: 母[はは]は弟[おとうと]に部屋[へや]を{掃除[そうじ]させました}。
examples.en: My mother made my younger brother clean his room.

examples.jp: 子[こ]どもを一人[ひとり]で買[か]い物[もの]に{行[い]かせました}。
examples.en: I sent my child shopping alone.

examples.jp: 遅[おく]れて、友達[ともだち]を三十分[さんじゅっぷん]も{待[ま]たせてしまった}。
examples.en: I was late and kept my friend waiting for thirty minutes.

examples.jp: 駅[えき]で一時間[いちじかん]も{待[ま]たされた}。
examples.en: I was kept waiting at the station for a whole hour.

examples.jp: 子[こ]どものころ、母[はは]に毎日[まいにち]ピアノを{練習[れんしゅう]させられました}。
examples.en: When I was a child, my mother made me practise the piano every day.

examples.jp: 飲[の]み会[かい]で先輩[せんぱい]にお酒[さけ]を{飲[の]まされた}。
examples.en: At the drinking party, a senior colleague made me drink.

contrast.note: 書かせた: I made someone write. 書かれた: someone wrote it, and it was done to me or to the thing.
食べさせた: I made someone eat. 食べさせられた: I was made to eat. Check who is the subject and who takes に.
行かせる is 'make or let go'; 行ける is 'can go'. Neither replaces the other.

mistakes.bad: 私[わたし]は母[はは]に野菜[やさい]を{食[た]べさせました}。
mistakes.good: 私[わたし]は母[はは]に野菜[やさい]を{食[た]べさせられました}。
mistakes.note: For 'I was made to eat', the subject is the one forced, so the verb needs causative + られる.

mistakes.bad: 友達[ともだち]を一時間[いちじかん]{待[ま]たれてしまった}。
mistakes.good: 友達[ともだち]を一時間[いちじかん]{待[ま]たせてしまった}。
mistakes.note: 'I kept my friend waiting' is the causative: I caused my friend to wait.

mistakes.bad: 部長[ぶちょう]に長[なが]い時間[じかん]{話[はな]さされました}。
mistakes.good: 部長[ぶちょう]に長[なが]い時間[じかん]{話[はな]させられました}。
mistakes.note: Verbs ending in す never take the short -asareru form.

skills.tip: Two people, one action: the causer is the subject (させる), or the one forced is the subject (させられる). Ask who wanted it.

skills.rule: Causative て-form + ください = 'please let me do it' (I act, you allow); + もらう = 'I was allowed to, and I am grateful'.
skills.explain:
させてください is the causative て-form + ください: literally 'please let me'. The speaker acts; the listener only gives permission. 私に払わせてください, 'let me pay'; 少し考えさせてください, 'let me think about it'. Compare 払ってください, which asks the listener to pay.

させてもらう says you were given permission and are grateful: 父に車を使わせてもらった, 'my father let me use the car'. The one who allows takes に. With the allower as subject it is させてくれる: 父が車を使わせてくれた. In polite speech, させていただく announces your own action humbly: 明日は休ませていただきます. This is different from させられる, which means you were forced.

Build the causative correctly: godan 休む→休ませて, 帰る→帰らせて, 言う→言わせて; ichidan 考える→考えさせて; する→させて. 休みさせて and 帰りさせて are wrong.
patterns: [allower] に [causative て-form] もらう / いただく

examples.jp: ここは私[わたし]に{払[はら]わせてください}。
examples.en: Please let me pay this time.

examples.jp: 少[すこ]し{考[かんが]えさせてください}。
examples.en: Please let me think about it a little.

examples.jp: 気分[きぶん]が悪[わる]いので、早[はや]く{帰[かえ]らせてください}。
examples.en: I feel unwell, so please let me go home early.

examples.jp: 父[ちち]に車[くるま]を{使[つか]わせてもらいました}。
examples.en: My father let me use his car.

examples.jp: 店長[てんちょう]に頼[たの]んで、一日[いちにち]{休[やす]ませてもらいました}。
examples.en: I asked the manager and was allowed to take a day off.

examples.jp: それでは、新[あたら]しい計画[けいかく]について説明[せつめい]{させていただきます}。
examples.en: Now, allow me to explain the new plan.

contrast.note: 払ってください: you pay. 払わせてください: let me pay.
使わせてもらった: I was allowed to use it (glad). 使わせられた: I was made to use it (not glad).
父に車を洗ってもらった: my father washed the car for me. 父に車を洗わせてもらった: my father let me wash it.

mistakes.bad: ここは私[わたし]が{払[はら]ってください}。
mistakes.good: ここは私[わたし]に{払[はら]わせてください}。
mistakes.note: てください asks the listener to act; to ask to act yourself, use the causative.

mistakes.bad: 父[ちち]に車[くるま]を{使[つか]わせられました}。
mistakes.good: 父[ちち]に車[くるま]を{使[つか]わせてもらいました}。
mistakes.note: させられる means you were forced; for a favour you were allowed, use させてもらう.

mistakes.bad: 先生[せんせい]、明日[あした]{休[やす]みさせてください}。
mistakes.good: 先生[せんせい]、明日[あした]{休[やす]ませてください}。
mistakes.note: 休む is godan: its causative is 休ませる. Do not attach させる to the stem.

skills.tip: Who does the verb? If it is me and I need someone's OK, use させてください (asking) or させてもらった (received).

skills.rule: ないで / ずに = without doing, instead of doing (how the next action is done); なくて = because of not doing (a cause or a feeling follows).
skills.explain:
All three negate a verb and join it to what follows, but they are not interchangeable. ないで tells how the next action is done or what is done instead: 朝ご飯を食べないで出かけた, 'I went out without eating breakfast'; バスに乗らないで歩いた, 'I walked instead of taking the bus'. It also makes negative requests: 触らないでください.

ずに means the same as this ないで and sounds more written or formal: 何も言わずに帰った. Form it from the ない stem: 食べずに, 行かずに; する becomes せずに, never しずに. It does not replace なくて for a cause (written style uses ず alone: 分からず、困った), and there is no ずにください.

なくて gives a cause: the first clause is why the second happened, or why you feel as you do: 意味が分からなくて困った; バスが来なくて遅刻した. Adjectives and nouns have only なくて (高くなくて, 学生じゃなくて), and the set patterns なくてもいい and なくてはいけない always use なくて.
patterns: [ない form] で [main action] (without / instead of)
[ない stem] なくて、[result / feeling] (because not)
[ない form] でください (please don't)

examples.jp: 朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を{食[た]べないで}学校[がっこう]に行[い]きました。
examples.en: I went to school without eating breakfast.

examples.jp: ここで写真[しゃしん]を{撮[と]らないでください}。
examples.en: Please don't take photos here.

examples.jp: 漢字[かんじ]が{読[よ]めなくて}、困[こま]りました。
examples.en: I couldn't read the kanji, so I was stuck.

examples.jp: 宿題[しゅくだい]が{終[お]わらなくて}、昨夜[ゆうべ]は遅[おそ]くまで起[お]きていた。
examples.en: I couldn't finish my homework, so I stayed up late last night.

examples.jp: 辞書[じしょ]を{使[つか]わずに}、この本[ほん]を読[よ]みました。
examples.en: I read this book without using a dictionary.

examples.jp: 兄[あに]は何[なに]も{言[い]わずに}部屋[へや]を出[で]ていった。
examples.en: My older brother left the room without saying anything.

contrast.vs: ないで vs なくて
contrast.note: 傘を持たないで出かけた: I went out without an umbrella (manner). 傘がなくて濡れた: I had no umbrella, so I got wet (cause).
Same meaning (without / instead of); ずに is more written. For a cause use なくて, not ずに; ずに cannot end a request.
なくても is 'even if not': 行かなくてもいい, 'you don't have to go'. It concedes; it is not a cause.

mistakes.bad: 意味[いみ]が{分[わ]からないで}、困[こま]りました。
mistakes.good: 意味[いみ]が{分[わ]からなくて}、困[こま]りました。
mistakes.note: Not understanding is the cause of the trouble, so use なくて.

mistakes.bad: 傘[かさ]を{持[も]たなくて}出[で]かけました。
mistakes.good: 傘[かさ]を{持[も]たないで}出[で]かけました。
mistakes.note: This says how you went out (without an umbrella), so use ないで or ずに.

mistakes.bad: 何[なに]も{しずに}帰[かえ]りました。
mistakes.good: 何[なに]も{せずに}帰[かえ]りました。
mistakes.note: The ずに form of する is せずに.

skills.tip: Can you put 'without' in the English? ないで or ずに. Can you put 'so' between the clauses? なくて.
